population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 63.6M of ~266M US adults are currently on an incretin (23.9%). Age check: 0.20×14 + 0.33×24 + 0.24×36 + 0.23×20 ≈ 23.96. Income thirds (19.5/24/28) average ≈ 23.8. The bottom third grew most in proportional terms (12→19.5) because of the 2029 gray-market flood and then the $39–59 legal generic. No new payer covers it; this is cash at a lower price. Cycling: ever 31% − current 23.9% = 7.1 pp of adults (~18.9M) have used and are off now. About 30% of current users are restarters (0.30×23.9 ≈ 7.2 pp), a lower share than 2028's 35% because ~7 pp of adults were first-time starters in the window. About 25% of those off now had cycled before (0.25×7.1 ≈ 1.8 pp), so (7.2+1.8)/31 ≈ 29% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once. Of the ~18.9M who are off, ~6M stopped for coverage reasons, ~5M for GI or other side effects, ~2M after counterfeit scares or the NAION label, and the rest by choice or at a goal weight. Payer mix of 63.6M current users: diabetes/cardiac-coded across all payers ~21M; employer obesity coverage ~8.5M; Medicare Continuity Model ~1.8M; Medicaid obesity ~1.6M; brand cash via TrumpRx/direct ~9M; US generic or authorised-generic semaglutide cash ~14M; gray market ~7.7M. These sum to 63.6M. Within those, ~3.5M are adults with BMI <27 and no diabetes on low-dose 'metabolic health' regimens, mostly generic cash or gray, and ~1.2M are normal-weight people using it off-label for nicotine cessation. Pediatric: ~1.1% of under-18s (~0.8M), almost all aged 12+, skewed to insured upper-income families. About one US child in three now lives in a household where an adult is on the drug. The never-users who can't afford even $39 are a smaller group than in 2028, but they are concentrated among the uninsured in the rural South and among adults with no bank card for telehealth checkout.

access.public_coverage: Structurally unchanged. Medicare: the CMS GLP-1 Continuity Model still pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 copay and keeps the ≥80% PDC refill rule, the ≥5%-at-6-months response rule and the 12-month lockout. About 1.8M obesity-only beneficiaries are enrolled: 1.8M × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.3B/yr. Medicaid: the same 19 states cover obesity at the $245 rate for ~1.6M enrollees: 1.6M × $245 × 12 ≈ $4.7B gross, federal share at ~65% FMAP ≈ $3.1B. Seven of them keep adherence waivers. Neither programme has repriced for generic semaglutide, which reached full multi-source entry only in Oct 2030. A few states began routine generic substitution in Q4 2030, but the savings are not yet visible in any budget and are not counted here.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India has 70+ generic semaglutide brands at ~$6–35/month, and generic oral semaglutide is on Indian shelves since 2028. Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, China and most of Southeast Asia have injectable generics. Chinese peptide labs now supply both licensed generic makers and the counterfeit trade.
access.note: The generic collapse is a semaglutide event, not a class event. Novo settled patent litigation in Nov 2029. It launched an authorised generic of injectable semaglutide in Mar 2030 at $59/month, and licensed generic entrants (Viatris, Teva, Sandoz) launched in Oct 2030. Warehouse clubs and cost-plus pharmacies now sell it at $39–49. Tirzepatide, retatrutide and orforglipron stay brand-only: Zepbound is $199–249 direct, retatrutide was cut to $349, and Foundayo and the Wegovy pill start at $149 on TrumpRx. Employer coverage is flat at 43%, with most of it still code-restricted, and about half of covering plans now require generic semaglutide first. BMI surcharges persist at ~1 in 5 large self-funded employers, and wellness vendors accept refill data or clip-on smart caps as proof of adherence. Gray market: personal-importation telehealth plus counterfeit and research-peptide product peaked at ~9M users in mid-2029, during the gap between demand and legal cheap supply. It is falling but sits at ~7.7M at end-2030. The remaining demand is research-peptide retatrutide (still cheaper than the brand at $120–200), 'stacks' and counterfeits that copy generic packaging. New starts are ~30% oral; the cheap generic pulled new starts back toward weekly injection.

drugs.pipeline_note: Muscle-preserving combination (driver next_gen_launch): Lilly's bimagrumab + tirzepatide was not in the 2028 pipeline note as a late-stage asset, so it cannot be on the US market by end-2030. The driver is realised by the BLA filing (Sep 2029) on phase 3 data in which lean mass made up ~10% of weight lost against ~35% on tirzepatide alone. The FDA granted priority review, with a PDUFA date in Q1 2031. Lilly's investor day and the press have already presented the 'skinny-frail' problem as solved; label, price and long-term safety are unknown. Amycretin (Novo) was filed in Q2 2029 and is under review with a decision expected 2031. Survodutide (BI) was filed in Q1 2029 and is still under review after a manufacturing information request. MariTide (Amgen, monthly) was filed in Jun 2030 and is not approved. Semaglutide's AUD phase 3 read out positive in 2029, the sNDA was filed in Apr 2030, and a decision is due 2031. The global incretin market is ~$135B in 2030: volume is up sharply, per-unit revenue is down, Novo's US semaglutide revenue is eroding through its own authorised generic, and Lilly's share is above 55%.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading side-effect cause of discontinuation. Unsupervised titration on cheap generic and gray product has increased ER visits for dehydration.
Elevated with rapid loss, especially on retatrutide.
No causal confirmation in long RCTs; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; the MDL's first bellwether trial was set for 2031, with no verdicts yet.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Further cohorts associate long-term use in women over 60 with lower bone density. The bimagrumab combination data recast this as 'solvable', but it is not yet solved for anyone outside a trial.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Retatrutide label advice unchanged; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A 2029–30 pooled analysis of RCT safety databases plus FDA Sentinel and Nordic registries found a hazard roughly doubled across the class, with an absolute excess of ~1–2 per 10,000 person-years. It is higher with diabetes and in the first year of therapy. Most cases are unilateral, and visual loss is mostly permanent.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class Warning and Precaution for all GLP-1 RA–containing products (Jun 2030), with a Medication Guide update and advice to seek urgent care for sudden vision loss. Ophthalmology societies recommend a baseline eye history but no routine screening. EMA updated its frequency to 'rare'.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still unquantified. The new users are normal-weight people on low 'longevity' doses and young vapers, who have no disease against which to weigh an effect, and they describe 'less noise' and 'a quieter head' as wellness. The AUD programme measured craving, not hedonic tone.
About half of lost weight returns within a year. Coverage stops are still the commonest cause of discontinuation, and cheap generics now let many people restart within weeks instead of months.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; it still underpins the Medicare and Medicaid adherence rules.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: More reports at retatrutide-level intake reduction and in low-BMI longevity users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; societies recommend baseline and annual labs.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; adolescents; repeated on/off cycling

safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; the Sentinel cycling study is ongoing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: In 2029 two problems overlapped. Counterfeit pens containing insulin caused severe hypoglycaemia, and contaminated vials caused Burkholderia and endotoxin infections. CDC counted ~410 hospitalisations and 11 deaths across 17 states by early 2030. FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~11,000 cumulative. Counterfeits now copy legitimate generic packaging.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: CDC Health Alert (May 2029), FDA warning letters and import alerts under existing authority. Personal-importation enforcement is still mostly unpursued.

safety_ledger.effect: Acquired olfactory and taste dysfunction after ≥5 years of continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A second cohort (UK CPRD, 2029) found a smaller HR of ~1.3, with confounding by diabetes duration still unresolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA PRAC added 'hyposmia' as uncommon to EU semaglutide product information (2029). FDA has made no label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Mostly mild and dose-related; more common with gray-market retatrutide at untitrated doses.

safety_ledger.effect: Unknown risk–benefit in low-dose use by adults without obesity or diabetes
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About 3.5M users with no outcome trials. They carry the new NAION warning and the lean-mass and nutrition concerns with no disease benefit yet demonstrated.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. The use is off-label prescribing by licensed telehealth clinicians, and it is legal.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~35% of US households. Snack and confectionery unit volumes are down a further ~2–3% (about 6% below 2026), and sugary drinks are down a further ~2%. Protein, fibre and small-format SKUs keep growing. Private-label snack makers are closing two more Midwest plants. The CPG firms that adapted early report flat-to-slightly-up value sales.

alcohol.state: Spirits volumes are down a further ~3% and beer is down ~2%; low/no-ABV is growing. Tobacco feels the effect most clearly: cigarette volume declines are ~2 points faster than the pre-2028 trend, and vape-pod sales to under-30s have fallen. Altria and PMI cite incretins in earnings calls, not only in risk factors.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat and tickets are held up by premium small plates. Half-portion menus are standard. Buffet closures continue. Bars near college campuses report weaker late-night trade.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting. The body-politics revival supports a small 'unmedicated' indie-brand niche. Returns and re-buying from people cycling on and off the drug remain a cost line for mainstream retailers.

fitness.state: Strength and 'lean-mass' studios are growing; chains such as Life Time and franchise strength gyms bundle DEXA scans. The bimagrumab filing gives them a new pitch ('stay strong until the combo comes'). The research-peptide stack trade runs through gym culture.

insurance.state: Structurally unchanged: coverage is concentrated on diabetes and cardiac codes, and employer obesity coverage is ~43%. Generic semaglutide lowers costs on the diabetes-coded side; pharmacy trend moderates to ~6%. Employers that dropped obesity coverage have not reinstated it, arguing that a $39 drug is now affordable out of pocket. BMI surcharges persist.

pharma.state: Volume is growing fast and price per unit is falling. Lilly is dominant on brand-only tirzepatide and retatrutide. Novo keeps US semaglutide volume through its authorised generic but loses revenue, and announces another round of cost cuts. Viatris, Teva and Sandoz gain a high-volume, low-margin product. Indian and Chinese API makers sell to both the legitimate and the counterfeit supply chains.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: At $39 a month, a larger body no longer reads as a coverage gap. Increasingly it reads as a choice, or as refusal, which makes being fat more legible as an identity and more exposed to moral judgment. Lean, muscled thinness after 40 is the new upper-class mark: drug plus trainer plus DEXA scan. 'Reta face' now has a counterpart, 'skinny-soft', for loss without lifting.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The tiers have compressed on price and widened on quality. Professionals get brand tirzepatide or retatrutide with coverage, trainers and labs. The working middle gets $39–49 generic semaglutide from Costco with no monitoring. The poorest and the undocumented still buy gray product, which is where the counterfeits land. On-drug rates are 28% in the top income third and 19.5% in the bottom.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Split tables at potlucks are normal. In Texas and Oklahoma the 'Made Whole' congregations hold monthly 'Full Table Sundays', and in Atlanta's West End a Black-church and fat-liberation coalition runs an annual 'Second Helpings' festival. Workplace catering defaults to small plates.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Apps in large cities add optional 'GLP-1' filters. 'Unmedicated' has become a self-description on profiles in Austin and Oakland, used in roughly the way 'sober' or 'vegan' is used. Mismatched appetite in couples is a standard topic for couples therapists.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: The appetite debate has become a values debate. When the drug cost $300, refusing it was ambiguous; at $39 it reads as a statement. The backlash coalition of fat liberation, evangelical 'Made Whole' and MAHA-style 'natural body' groups gained recruits from the counterfeit deaths and the vision warning. Its factions still disagree on whether the problem is pharma, vanity or sin.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: No instrument measures it in any trial, registry or label. The growth is among people who are not ill. Healthy longevity users and young ex-vapers describe 'less mental noise' as a benefit in forum posts and on wellness podcasts, but no clinician or company has claimed it as an effect, so it stays anecdote.
interior_life.framing: Treatment and character. Quieter wanting is called discipline, recovery or 'regulation'. Among longevity users it is called 'clarity'.
interior_life.effect_on_work: HR anecdotes about steady, low-drama staff persist. Some trading desks and sales floors joke about 'semaglutide calm'. Wellness vendors report fewer smoke breaks among hourly workers on the drug. Nothing is written down as an effect of the drug.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Campus bars and late-night gaming groups report thinner turnout among under-30s, attributed to vape quitting and cost. High-intensity live formats (immersive raves, extreme-sauna clubs) keep growing. Some indie musicians release 'unmedicated' records as a genre stance.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Therapist podcasts discuss couples in which one partner is on a longevity dose and 'content'. The clinical literature is silent.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable turnout effect. 'Sedated workforce' rhetoric is a staple of the backlash coalition, which makes the question politically coded and keeps it unfunded.

state.regulatory_posture: Unchanged in structure; no new state action this window. The FDA applied its existing authority: the NAION class label, warning letters and import alerts after the counterfeit cluster. Its posture toward personal importation is still passive. The administration takes credit for the cheap generic, which came from a private settlement, while its MAHA wing amplifies the counterfeit deaths and the eye warning.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Continuity Model, the 19 Medicaid states and TrumpRx continue on 2028 terms. Neither programme has repriced to generic levels.

Because cheap generic pens are not connected, wellness vendors sell $10–15 clip-on smart caps that report injection events, which extends adherence data to cash-pay users who want the waiver. Texas's 2027 ban still covers only state-regulated plans.
state.workforce_or_military: Army and Air Force accession waivers (≥6 months off-drug stability) are unchanged. TRICARE covers active duty only. Recruiters report more applicants disclosing prior use.

prose.headline: The $39 Shot: Weight Loss Got Cheap, the Fakes Got Deadly, and the Label Now Warns About Your Eyes
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 nearly one American adult in four takes an incretin drug, about 64 million people, and almost 19 million more have taken one and stopped. The most important change of the past two years is the price. Coverage rules barely moved. Since October a box of generic semaglutide costs $39 to $49 at a warehouse club. Novo Nordisk settled its patent fights and launched its own unbranded version at $59 in March, a few months ahead of the generics it had licensed. The rest of the class did not get cheap. Tirzepatide is still brand-only at around $200. Retatrutide, the triple agonist that takes off nearly 30 percent of body weight, now costs $349. The new question is what kind of drug a person can afford, and with what supervision.

Coverage rules stayed as they were. Employers that stopped paying for obesity drugs have not resumed, and some now say a $39 drug is a household expense. Medicare still pays $245 a month for covered beneficiaries who refill on time and lose five percent in six months, and still locks out for a year those who don't. Nineteen Medicaid states do the same. Neither has yet noticed that the molecule sells for a sixth of that price at Costco. Employers that charge BMI surcharges still waive them for adherence, and since cheap generic pens are not connected, wellness vendors now sell plastic caps that report each injection.

The price fell after a bad year. In 2029, before legal generics arrived, demand ran ahead of cheap legal supply, and counterfeit pens filled the gap. Some contained insulin, and others carried bacteria. The CDC counted about 410 hospitalisations and eleven deaths, mostly among people who had bought through social media because $199 was too much. The gray market has shrunk since, but counterfeiters now copy the packaging of the legitimate generics.

In June the FDA put a vision warning on every drug in the class. Pooled trial and registry data showed that the optic-nerve stroke called NAION, once listed as very rare, occurs at roughly twice the background rate. The absolute risk is still small, one or two extra cases per ten thousand patient-years. The warning lands on a population that now includes millions of people who are not sick. Telehealth companies sell $49 low-dose 'metabolic health' plans to lean professionals who want to stay lean, and 'quit vaping' plans to people in their twenties. About three and a half million adults with no obesity and no diabetes take the drug for wellness. No outcome trial covers them.

The frailty problem, muscle lost along with fat, has been declared solved before it is approved. Lilly filed a combination of tirzepatide and bimagrumab, a muscle-preserving antibody, after trials in which almost all the weight lost was fat. A decision is due in early 2031. Strength gyms advertise that people should hold on until it arrives. In the meantime, gym forums sell unapproved peptides that claim to do the same thing.

The counter-movement grew on these events. In August thousands of 'Made Whole' congregations in Texas and Oklahoma signed a covenant to eat as God made them. In the same weekend about 40,000 people crowded Atlanta's West End for a fat-liberation festival with Black church choirs. They did not share a stage. Because the drug costs $39, a larger body reads as a choice, which makes it easier to celebrate and easier to judge.

Snack volumes are down a few more points, spirits and beer are down, and cigarette sales are falling faster than they used to. Nothing has collapsed. Users describe 'less noise' and call it clarity. Nobody measures it.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Tanya Brill clocks in at the Groveport fulfilment centre at 5:52, eight minutes early, because the scanners lag. At first break she checks the WellPath app. The little grey cap on her pen logged Sunday's shot, and the line under her name reads SURCHARGE WAIVED: ADHERENT, which is $85 back each month.

The pen is the Costco one now, $44, a white box with a plain blue stripe. Last year it was a seller on Instagram until her cousin Dee ended up at Grant Medical shaking and grey with an insulin pen inside a fake label. Tanya threw out the two she had left. She remembers standing over the kitchen trash for a long time.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and gives the other half to Marcus, who isn't on anything and says so the way some people say they don't drink.

The pharmacist's new leaflet is folded in her locker. One paragraph is in bold: sudden loss of vision in one eye, go to the emergency room. She read it twice and then covered one eye in the break-room mirror, feeling stupid, and then the other.

At home her mother calls from Tulsa about Full Table Sunday at the church and asks if Tanya will come at Thanksgiving and actually eat. Tanya says yes. She means it, mostly.

Her son Jaden, fifteen, is on the couch with a vape he thinks she can't smell. She thinks about the quit-vaping ads, the $49 ones, and decides not tonight.

In bed her husband asks if she's okay. She says she's fine, that it's just quiet in her head lately, that quiet is good.
